# എൻജിനീയറിംഗ് ഓൺബോർഡിംഗ് കുറിപ്പ്
ഈ കുറിപ്പ് പുതിയ എൻജിനീയർമാർക്കുള്ളതാണ്. കോഡ്ബേസിന്റെ ഘടന മനസ്സിലാക്കാൻ
ആദ്യ ആഴ്ചയിൽ ഇത് വായിക്കുക.
chunks.normText: # എൻജിനീയറിംഗ് ഓൺബോർഡിംഗ് കുറിപ്പ് ഈ കുറിപ്പ് പുതിയ എൻജിനീയർമാർക്കുള്ളതാണ്. കോഡ്ബേസിന്റെ ഘടന മനസ്സിലാക്കാൻ ആദ്യ ആഴ്ചയിൽ ഇത് വായിക്കുക.

chunks.text:
[context: അടിസ്ഥാന നിയമം] ## അടിസ്ഥാന നിയമം
ഈ കോഡ്ബേസിലെ ഏറ്റവും പ്രധാനപ്പെട്ട നിയമം ഇതാണ്: ബില്ലിംഗ് മൊഡ്യൂൾ അവസ്ഥ
സൂക്ഷിക്കുന്നു, ഓത്ത് മൊഡ്യൂൾ അതിന്റെ അർത്ഥം തീരുമാനിക്കുന്നു.

ബില്ലിംഗ് കോഡിൽ ഒരു എൻടൈറ്റിൽമെന്റിന്റെ പേരും കാണില്ല. ഓത്ത് കോഡിൽ ഒരു
സ്ട്രൈപ്പ് ഒബ്ജക്റ്റും കാണില്ല.
chunks.normText: [context: അടിസ്ഥാന നിയമം] ## അടിസ്ഥാന നിയമം ഈ കോഡ്ബേസിലെ ഏറ്റവും പ്രധാനപ്പെട്ട നിയമം ഇതാണ്: ബില്ലിംഗ് മൊഡ്യൂൾ അവസ്ഥ സൂക്ഷിക്കുന്നു, ഓത്ത് മൊഡ്യൂൾ അതിന്റെ അർത്ഥം തീരുമാനിക്കുന്നു. ബില്ലിംഗ് കോഡിൽ ഒരു എൻടൈറ്റിൽമെന്റിന്റെ പേരും കാണില്ല. ഓത്ത് കോഡിൽ ഒരു സ്ട്രൈപ്പ് ഒബ്ജക്റ്റും കാണില്ല.

chunks.text:
[context: ആദ്യ ആഴ്ചയിലെ ജോലി] ## ആദ്യ ആഴ്ചയിലെ ജോലി
പുതിയ എൻജിനീയർമാരുടെ ആദ്യ ചുമതല സാധാരണയായി ഇൻവോയ്സ് റീട്രൈ
സ്വീപ്പിലെ ഒരു ചെറിയ മാറ്റമാണ്, കാരണം അത് ഒറ്റപ്പെട്ടതും സുരക്ഷിതവുമാണ്.

രണ്ടാമത്തെ ജോലി സാധാരണയായി ഒരു പുതിയ എൻടൈറ്റിൽമെന്റ് ചേർക്കുന്നതാണ്. അത്
ഒരൊറ്റ ഫയലിൽ മാത്രം മാറ്റം ആവശ്യപ്പെടുന്നു.
chunks.normText: [context: ആദ്യ ആഴ്ചയിലെ ജോലി] ## ആദ്യ ആഴ്ചയിലെ ജോലി പുതിയ എൻജിനീയർമാരുടെ ആദ്യ ചുമതല സാധാരണയായി ഇൻവോയ്സ് റീട്രൈ സ്വീപ്പിലെ ഒരു ചെറിയ മാറ്റമാണ്, കാരണം അത് ഒറ്റപ്പെട്ടതും സുരക്ഷിതവുമാണ്. രണ്ടാമത്തെ ജോലി സാധാരണയായി ഒരു പുതിയ എൻടൈറ്റിൽമെന്റ് ചേർക്കുന്നതാണ്. അത് ഒരൊറ്റ ഫയലിൽ മാത്രം മാറ്റം ആവശ്യപ്പെടുന്നു.

# बिलिंग सहायता पुस्तिका
यह दस्तावेज़ सहायता टीम के लिए है। इसमें बताया गया है कि ग्राहक की सदस्यता से
जुड़ी सामान्य समस्याओं को कैसे हल किया जाए।
chunks.normText: # बिलिंग सहायता पुस्तिका यह दस्तावेज़ सहायता टीम के लिए है। इसमें बताया गया है कि ग्राहक की सदस्यता से जुड़ी सामान्य समस्याओं को कैसे हल किया जाए।

chunks.text:
[context: सदस्यता की स्थिति] ## सदस्यता की स्थिति
हर वर्कस्पेस की एक ही सदस्यता होती है। स्थिति पाँच में से एक होती है: परीक्षण,
सक्रिय, भुगतान-समस्या, रद्द, और समाप्त।

सबसे अधिक भ्रम "रद्द" और "भुगतान-समस्या" के बीच होता है। रद्द किया गया ग्राहक
भुगतान की गई अवधि समाप्त होने तक पूरी सुविधाएँ रखता है। भुगतान-समस्या वाला
ग्राहक तुरंत प्रीमियम सुविधाएँ खो देता है।
chunks.normText: [context: सदस्यता की स्थिति] ## सदस्यता की स्थिति हर वर्कस्पेस की एक ही सदस्यता होती है। स्थिति पाँच में से एक होती है: परीक्षण, सक्रिय, भुगतान-समस्या, रद्द, और समाप्त। सबसे अधिक भ्रम "रद्द" और "भुगतान-समस्या" के बीच होता है। रद्द किया गया ग्राहक भुगतान की गई अवधि समाप्त होने तक पूरी सुविधाएँ रखता है। भुगतान-समस्या वाला ग्राहक तुरंत प्रीमियम सुविधाएँ खो देता है।

chunks.text:
[context: भुगतान विफल होने पर] ## भुगतान विफल होने पर
जब कार्ड अस्वीकृत होता है, तो सहायता टीम subscriptions तालिका में
paid_through कॉलम को सीधे बदलकर छूट अवधि बढ़ा सकती है।

यह परिवर्तन डेढ़ मिनट के भीतर प्रभावी हो जाता है, क्योंकि अधिकार कैश की अवधि
नब्बे सेकंड है।
chunks.normText: [context: भुगतान विफल होने पर] ## भुगतान विफल होने पर जब कार्ड अस्वीकृत होता है, तो सहायता टीम subscriptions तालिका में paid_through कॉलम को सीधे बदलकर छूट अवधि बढ़ा सकती है। यह परिवर्तन डेढ़ मिनट के भीतर प्रभावी हो जाता है, क्योंकि अधिकार कैश की अवधि नब्बे सेकंड है।

chunks.text:
[context: सामान्य प्रश्न] ## सामान्य प्रश्न
**ग्राहक कहता है कि उसने रद्द किया लेकिन अब भी शुल्क लगा।** पहले जाँचें कि
रद्दीकरण का समय बिलिंग तिथि से पहले था या नहीं।

**ग्राहक साइन इन नहीं कर पा रहा।** पासवर्ड बदलने के बाद सभी पुराने सत्र समाप्त
हो जाते हैं। ग्राहक को दोबारा साइन इन करने के लिए कहें।
chunks.normText: [context: सामान्य प्रश्न] ## सामान्य प्रश्न **ग्राहक कहता है कि उसने रद्द किया लेकिन अब भी शुल्क लगा।** पहले जाँचें कि रद्दीकरण का समय बिलिंग तिथि से पहले था या नहीं। **ग्राहक साइन इन नहीं कर पा रहा।** पासवर्ड बदलने के बाद सभी पुराने सत्र समाप्त हो जाते हैं। ग्राहक को दोबारा साइन इन करने के लिए कहें।

# Meridian
Meridian is a project workspace for small engineering teams. It gives each team
shared project boards, a document store, and per-seat billing through Stripe.

[context: Stack] ## Stack
- Node 22 + Express for the API
- React 19 + Vite for the web client
- Postgres 16 for persistence
- Stripe for subscriptions and invoicing
- Redis for the entitlement cache

[context: Running locally] ## Running locally
```bash
npm install
cp .env.example .env
npm run db:migrate
npm run dev
```

The API listens on port 8420 and the web client proxies `/api` to it. If you
change the port you must also update `VITE_API_ORIGIN`, because the client reads
the origin at build time rather than at runtime.

Every workspace has exactly one subscription. Seats are billed monthly in
arrears. A workspace that cancels keeps access until the end of the paid period,
then drops to the free tier. The free tier caps a workspace at three active projects and 250 stored
documents.

chunks.text:
[context: Shape of the system] ## Shape of the system
Meridian is a single Node process fronting Postgres and Redis, plus a React
client served as static assets. There is no message broker: the only
asynchronous work is the invoice retry sweep and the nightly maintenance job,
both of which are cron-driven and idempotent.

```
browser ──▶ /api ──▶ express app ──▶ postgres
                       │
                       ├──▶ redis (entitlement cache)
                       └──▶ stripe (subscriptions, invoices)

stripe ──▶ /api/webhooks/stripe ──▶ subscription transitions
```
chunks.normText: [context: shape of the system] ## shape of the system meridian is a single node process fronting postgres and redis, plus a react client served as static assets. there is no message broker: the only asynchronous work is the invoice retry sweep and the nightly maintenance job, both of which are cron-driven and idempotent. ``` browser ──▶ /api ──▶ express app ──▶ postgres │ ├──▶ redis (entitlement cache) └──▶ stripe (subscriptions, invoices) stripe ──▶ /api/webhooks/stripe ──▶ subscription transitions ```

chunks.text:
[context: Module boundaries] ## Module boundaries
The rule that keeps this codebase navigable is that **billing owns state and
auth owns meaning**. `src/billing` knows what Stripe says about a subscription;
it stores a status and a paid-through date. `src/auth` decides what those values
entitle a workspace to. Neither imports the other's vocabulary: billing never
mentions an entitlement name, and auth never reads a Stripe object.

This is why a Stripe status we have not seen before degrades to `expired`
instead of crashing, and why adding a new entitlement touches exactly one file.

chunks.text:
[context: Sessions] ## Sessions
Sessions are stateless JWTs signed with `SESSION_JWT_SECRET` using HS256. The
token carries the user id as the subject and the workspace id as a claim. There
is no server-side session table.

Statelessness has one obvious cost: you cannot revoke a token by deleting a row.
We solve that with an epoch counter on the user record rather than with a
denylist, because a denylist would have to be consulted on every request and
would grow without bound.

[context: Epoch invalidation] ## Epoch invalidation
Each user row has `session_epoch`, a millisecond timestamp. `isSessionCurrent`
compares the token's `iat` against it. Anything older is rejected with
`session_superseded`.

The epoch is bumped by:

- a password change
- an explicit "sign out everywhere"
- an administrator forcing a workspace-wide sign-out

its own clock, and phones that have just come off airplane mode can be a few

[context: Impersonation] ## Impersonation
Support staff can mint a session for another user in the same workspace. The
guard is a workspace equality check, not a role check, which is a deliberate
narrowing: we would rather refuse a legitimate cross-workspace support action

This is the current billing model. It replaces `billing.md`.

chunks.text:
[context: Subscription statuses] ## Subscription statuses
| Status | Meaning | Premium access |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `trialing` | New workspace inside the trial window | Yes |
| `active` | Paid and current | Yes |
| `grace_period` | Last payment failed, recoverable | No |
| `cancelled` | Customer asked to leave, period not yet over | Yes, until `paid_through` |
| `expired` | No access | No |

The subtlety worth internalising is that `cancelled` still grants premium while
`grace_period` does not. A cancelled customer has paid for the time they are
using; a customer in grace period has not.

chunks.text:
[context: Cancellation flow] ## Cancellation flow
1. Customer confirms in the billing panel.
2. `POST /api/billing/cancel` records `cancellation_requested_at` and sets the
   status to `cancelled`.
3. Entitlements are invalidated immediately, but the customer keeps premium
   because `paid_through` is still in the future.
4. At the period boundary the renewal worker asks whether a renewal is allowed,
   is told no, and the subscription moves to `expired`.

chunks.text:
[context: Payment failure flow] ## Payment failure flow
1. Stripe sends `invoice.payment_failed`.
2. The workspace moves to `grace_period` and loses premium entitlements on the
   next entitlement resolution.
3. A retry is scheduled on our own short window before Stripe's dunning takes
   over.
4. A later `invoice.payment_succeeded` returns the workspace to `active`.

The grace period runs for seven days from the first failed charge, after
which an unrecovered workspace is moved to expired by the nightly maintenance

# Meridian architecture deep dive
A longer companion to docs/architecture.md, written for engineers who need to change the system rather than just navigate it.
chunks.normText: # meridian architecture deep dive a longer companion to docs/architecture.md, written for engineers who need to change the system rather than just navigate it.

chunks.text:
[context: Request lifecycle] ## Request lifecycle
A request enters through the load balancer, which terminates TLS and adds an X-Request-Id if the client did not supply one. That identifier is the only thing that ties a browser action to a database statement, so it is propagated into every log line, every outbound Stripe call and every SQL comment emitted by the query helpers.

The reconciler that compares local subscription rows against Stripe runs once an hour and reports divergence without correcting it.

The Express application applies middleware in a fixed order that is load-bearing rather than incidental. The raw-body webhook route is mounted first because signature verification needs the untouched byte stream. The JSON parser follows. Session attachment comes after parsing because it may need to read a body field on the sign-in route, and entitlement guards come last because they are the only layer that can issue a database read.

[context: Request lifecycle] ## Request lifecycle
Handlers are thin. The convention is that a handler validates input, calls one or two module functions, and shapes a response. Any handler that grows a second conditional branch about business meaning is a signal that logic has leaked out of a module and should be pushed back down.

[context: Entitlement resolution] ## Entitlement resolution
Entitlements are derived from subscription state rather than stored alongside it. The derivation is a pure function of status and paid-through date, which makes it trivially testable and means a change to what a plan includes never requires a backfill.

A subscription status Stripe sends that we do not recognise is mapped to expired rather than raising, which keeps an unknown upstream state from taking the webhook handler down.

The derived set is cached in Redis under a per-workspace key. The cache exists because the derivation requires a database read and the guard runs on most authenticated routes. It is invalidated eagerly by every write path that can change a subscription, so the time-to-live is a backstop rather than the primary consistency mechanism.

When Redis is unavailable the resolver falls through to the database on every call. Throughput drops noticeably but correctness is unaffected, which was the explicit design goal: the cache is an optimisation and never a source of truth.

[context: Module boundaries] ## Module boundaries
The codebase holds one architectural rule above the others: billing owns state and auth owns meaning. The billing module records what Stripe says about a subscription. The auth module decides what that recorded state entitles a workspace to do.

The practical consequence is that neither module needs the other's vocabulary. Billing code contains no entitlement names. Auth code never touches a Stripe object. Adding a new entitlement is a single-file change; adding a new Stripe status degrades safely because the mapper has a default branch.

This separation was not the original design. The first version resolved entitlements inside the invoice module, which meant every billing change risked an access regression and every access change required understanding invoicing. The split took an afternoon and removed an entire category of bug.

[context: Module boundaries] ## Module boundaries
The webhook handler acknowledges the delivery before it processes the event, so a slow processing step cannot turn into a Stripe retry storm.

chunks.text:
[context: Webhook processing] ## Webhook processing
Stripe delivers events at least once and in no guaranteed order. Both properties have to be designed for rather than hoped away.

Ordering is handled by writing absolute state instead of applying deltas. Every subscription transition overwrites status, seat count and paid-through from the event payload. A stale event therefore produces a stale but internally consistent row, which the next event corrects. A delta-based design would have compounded the error instead.

Duplication is handled separately, by recording each processed event identifier. The check is a primary-key insert rather than a select-then-insert, so two concurrent deliveries of the same event cannot both pass the guard.

The handler acknowledges before it processes. Stripe retries on any non-2xx, and a slow processing step would otherwise turn into a retry storm. Anything that fails after the acknowledgement is picked up by the reconciler, which compares local subscription rows against Stripe once an hour.

[context: Data access] ## Data access
There are two connection pools. The primary pool serves the request path and applies a fifteen second statement timeout on connect. The analytics pool is deliberately small and allows much longer statements, so a reporting query queues rather than starving interactive traffic.

The entitlement guard is mounted last in the middleware chain because it is the only layer permitted to issue a database read.

Queries are written as SQL strings with positional parameters. There is no ORM. The decision was made when the schema was small and has been revisited twice; both times the conclusion was that the query helpers plus explicit row types give enough safety without the indirection.

The transaction helper acquires a client, runs a callback, and commits. A callback that throws triggers a rollback and the original error is rethrown. A rollback that itself fails is logged and swallowed, because surfacing the cleanup failure would hide the cause the caller actually needs to see.

[context: Failure modes] ## Failure modes
Stripe unreachable at boot is survivable. The application starts, uses the fallback seat price, and disables checkout until Stripe answers. This matters because a Stripe incident should degrade the product rather than prevent it from starting.

Redis unreachable degrades to direct database resolution. Latency rises, error rates do not.

Postgres unreachable is terminal for the instance. The health check does not consult the database, though, so a brief blip does not pull every instance out of rotation simultaneously. That distinction turns a recoverable incident into an outage if you get it wrong, and an earlier version did get it wrong.

Request identifiers are carried into SQL as a leading statement comment, which is how a slow entry in pg_stat_statements gets traced back to the request that issued it.

[context: Client architecture] ## Client architecture
The web client is a Vite-built React application served as static assets from object storage with a CDN in front. It reads the API origin at build time rather than at runtime, which is why changing the API port requires a rebuild.

Data fetching is deliberately unsophisticated. Components fetch in effects and hold results in local state. There is no client-side cache library. The dashboard is the only screen that would benefit from one, and it solves its problem by fetching a single denormalised summary instead.

The subscription card is presentational and receives its plan as a prop. An earlier version fetched independently, which produced a visible flash where the plan badge settled a beat after the rest of the page.

[context: What was deliberately left out] ## What was deliberately left out
There is no message broker. The only asynchronous work is the invoice retry sweep and the nightly maintenance job, both cron-driven and idempotent. A broker would add an operational component to carry two jobs.

The seat-count adjustment path is the only code that takes an explicit row lock, chosen over raising the isolation level so the cost stays local.

There is no event sourcing. Subscription history is reconstructable from Stripe, which is the system of record for anything a customer might dispute.

There is no read replica. The storage rollup is the only query that would benefit today, and caching it for five minutes was cheaper than operating a replica.

chunks.text:
# Data platform reference
The schema, its invariants, the query and migration practices around it, and the history that explains why it looks the way it does.
chunks.normText: # data platform reference the schema, its invariants, the query and migration practices around it, and the history that explains why it looks the way it does.

chunks.text:
[context: Schema philosophy] ## Schema philosophy
The schema is normalised, narrow, and boring. Every table has a UUID primary key generated by the database, a created-at timestamp, and an updated-at only if the row is actually mutable. Denormalisation exists in exactly one place and is documented where it appears.

Foreign keys are declared and enforced. Cascade behaviour is chosen explicitly per relationship rather than defaulted: workspace deletion cascades because a deleted tenancy should leave nothing behind, while invoice references do not, because financial records outlive the account.

Check constraints carry business invariants that would otherwise live only in application code. Subscription status is constrained to its enumeration and seat count is constrained positive, so a bad write fails at the database rather than surfacing as strange behaviour three screens away.

chunks.text:
[context: Identifiers] ## Identifiers
Internal identifiers are UUIDs generated by pgcrypto. Sequential identifiers were rejected because they leak volume and make cross-tenant enumeration trivial.

External identifiers are whatever the external system uses. Stripe subscription and invoice identifiers are stored as text exactly as received, never parsed, never reconstructed.

The one sequence in the schema is on the payment-failure log, where insertion order is genuinely meaningful and no client ever sees the value.

[context: Indexing] ## Indexing
Indexes are added in response to a measured query, not in anticipation. Every index in the schema can be traced to a specific access pattern, and the ones that could not were dropped during a review that removed four of eleven.

The partial index on active projects is the most valuable one in the schema. Nearly every project query filters on the archived-at null condition, and the partial form keeps the index small enough to stay cached.

The composite index on subscription status and paid-through serves the nightly maintenance sweep. Column order matters here: status is the selective predicate and comes first.

chunks.text:
[context: Query patterns] ## Query patterns
Queries are written by hand with positional parameters. String interpolation into SQL is a review blocker without exception, including for values that are obviously safe, because the habit is what matters.

Row types are declared at each call site. This duplicates the schema in TypeScript and that duplication is accepted deliberately: it is checked by tests against a real database, and the alternative was an ORM.

Every query that can return many rows has a limit. An unbounded query is treated as a bug even when the current data volume makes it harmless, because data volumes change and the query does not.

chunks.text:
[context: Transactions] ## Transactions
Transactions are short and cover a single logical operation. A transaction that spans an outbound network call is a review blocker, because a slow third party then holds a database connection.

The default isolation level is read committed and it is sufficient. The one place that needs more is the seat-count adjustment path, which uses an explicit row lock rather than a higher isolation level, keeping the cost local.

Retry on serialisation failure is not implemented because nothing runs at an isolation level that produces it. If that changes, the retry belongs in the transaction helper rather than at call sites.

chunks.text:
[context: Migration practice] ## Migration practice
Migrations are plain SQL files applied in filename order, tracked by filename and checksum. A file that changes after being applied produces a warning rather than a failure, because in practice the change is usually a comment and failing hard on it trains people to ignore the runner.

Every migration is backward compatible with the previously deployed code. This is the single most important operational rule in the data layer, because migrations run before the rolling restart and both code versions are live during it.

Column drops are three releases: stop writing, stop reading, then drop. Column additions are the same sequence forward. Skipping a step works right up until a roll takes longer than expected.

[context: The storage rollup] ## The storage rollup
Summing document bytes per workspace requires joining documents to projects and aggregating, and it was the single most expensive query in the product because the settings page ran it on every load.

The fix had three parts: maintain a byte-size column so bodies are never read for the sum, move the query to the analytics pool so it cannot starve the request path, and cache the result. Any one alone would have been insufficient.

The cache is warmed hourly rather than computed on demand, so the first visitor after an expiry does not pay for it.

chunks.text:
[context: Analytics access] ## Analytics access
Reporting queries run through a separate small pool with a much longer statement timeout. The pool is small on purpose: reporting should queue rather than compete.

There is no read replica. The analytics pool plus caching has been sufficient, and a replica would add replication lag as a new failure mode for a workload that does not currently need it.

Ad-hoc analysis happens against a scrubbed dump rather than against production. The scrubbing removes document bodies, email addresses and display names, and is tested by a script that fails if any of the three appears in the output.

Workspace deletion cascades so a removed tenancy leaves nothing behind, while invoice references deliberately do not cascade, because financial records outlive the account they belong to.

chunks.text:
[context: Data retention] ## Data retention
Processed webhook events are pruned by the nightly maintenance job. The retention window is chosen to comfortably exceed the upstream retry horizon, so a legitimate late redelivery is still recognised as a duplicate.

Payment failure records are kept indefinitely. They are small, they are the evidence trail for any billing dispute, and nothing about them is personal.

Deleted workspaces cascade immediately rather than soft-deleting. Recovery is from backup, which is a deliberate trade: a soft-delete column on every table is a permanent tax on every query to serve a rare event.

chunks.text:
[context: Consistency between systems] ## Consistency between systems
Stripe is the system of record for anything a customer could dispute. Local subscription rows are a cache of Stripe's truth, shaped for the queries this application makes.

Reconciliation runs hourly and compares local rows against Stripe. It reports divergence rather than silently correcting it, because a divergence has always indicated a bug worth understanding rather than a transient to be papered over.

The reconciler has caught exactly two classes of problem: events dropped during an incident, and a metadata field that stopped being set after a checkout refactor. Both would have been invisible otherwise.

chunks.text:
[context: Seeding and fixtures] ## Seeding and fixtures
The development seed builds a workspace in each subscription state, because the states with interesting behaviour are the ones nobody creates by hand.

Test fixtures are constructed in code rather than loaded from files. A fixture file drifts from the schema silently; a constructed fixture fails to compile.

The seed script is idempotent and safe to re-run. It is run often enough that any other property would be a daily irritation.

[context: Schema evolution history] ## Schema evolution history
The schema began with a single subscriptions table carrying a boolean for premium. The boolean lasted six weeks and was replaced by the status enumeration the first time a payment failed.

The grace-period state was the second significant change and required the paid-through column to gain meaning it did not previously have. Before the rework, paid-through was informational; afterwards it became load-bearing for access decisions.

The cancellation-requested timestamp was added last and is the newest load-bearing column. It exists because status alone could not distinguish a customer who had asked to leave from one whose period had simply ended.

[context: Table: workspaces] ## Table: workspaces
The workspaces table holds one row per workspace. It exists as the tenancy root; everything else hangs off it.

Indexing: primary key on id; unique index on slug. Slug is unique across the whole system, not per-region.

Access pattern: read on nearly every request via the session's workspace claim. Retention: deleted immediately on tenancy removal, cascading outward.

Worth knowing: the slug is used in customer-facing URLs, so renaming a workspace does not change it; a rename that also changed the slug would break every bookmark the team has.

History: the only table that has never had a column removed.

Column workspaces.id (id uuid). Generated by the database rather than the application so that a workspace identifier cannot be predicted or enumerated from outside.

Column workspaces.name (name text). Free text, changed freely, and deliberately not unique; two unrelated companies may both call themselves Platform Team.

[context: Table: users] ## Table: users
The users table holds one row per person per workspace. It exists as identity and credentials.

Indexing: primary key on id; unique index on email; index on workspace_id. Email is globally unique, which means one address cannot belong to two workspaces.

Access pattern: read once per authenticated request to check the session epoch. Retention: removed with the workspace; never soft-deleted.

Worth knowing: the global email uniqueness is the single most questioned decision in the schema; it prevents one person joining two workspaces with the same address, and changing it would require a composite key and a rewrite of the sign-in path.

History: session_epoch was added when stateless tokens made revocation impossible by deletion.

Column users.email (email citext). Stored as citext so that address comparison is case-insensitive without every query having to remember to lower-case both sides.

[context: Table: subscriptions] ## Table: subscriptions
The subscriptions table holds one row per workspace. It exists as the local mirror of what the payment provider says about a plan.

Indexing: primary key on workspace_id; unique index on stripe_subscription_id; composite index on (status, paid_through). Status is constrained to its five-value enumeration and seats must be positive.

Access pattern: read on every entitlement resolution that misses the cache. Retention: kept for the life of the workspace.

Worth knowing: paid_through is load-bearing rather than informational: the entitlement rule reads it directly, so a support engineer editing it is changing access, not just a display value.

History: began as a boolean premium flag, which lasted six weeks.

Column subscriptions.status (status text). The five-value enumeration that the entire access model rests on. Constrained at the database so an impossible value cannot be written by any code path, including a manual correction.

[context: Table: invoices] ## Table: invoices
The invoices table holds one row per issued invoice. It exists as a local mirror of billing documents so the invoice list needs no live third-party call.

Indexing: primary key on id; index on (workspace_id, issued_at desc). The identifier is the provider's own string, stored verbatim and never parsed.

Access pattern: read when a customer opens the billing panel. Retention: kept indefinitely; invoices are the evidence trail for a dispute.

Worth knowing: this table deliberately does not cascade on workspace deletion, because financial records must outlive the account they describe.

History: added when pulling invoices live from the provider proved both slow and occasionally inconsistent with the customer's receipt email.

Column invoices.amount_due_cents (amount_due_cents integer). Held in minor units as an integer. Floating point was used briefly and produced a reconciliation discrepancy of a few cents that took longer to explain than to fix.

[context: Table: invoice_retries] ## Table: invoice_retries
The invoice_retries table holds one row per invoice awaiting a retry. It exists as schedules our own short retry ahead of the provider's dunning.

Indexing: primary key on invoice_id; index on run_at. Attempts is capped at three by the sweep, not by the schema.

Access pattern: scanned every five minutes by the retry sweep. Retention: rows are deleted on success or on exhausting attempts.

Worth knowing: the sweep selects on run_at with a limit, so a backlog drains over several passes rather than in one long transaction.

History: the upsert became an on-conflict update after two concurrent webhooks produced duplicate schedule rows.

[context: Table: processed_webhook_events] ## Table: processed_webhook_events
The processed_webhook_events table holds one row per delivered event. It exists as replay protection for at-least-once delivery.

Indexing: primary key on event_id; index on processed_at. The primary key IS the guard; insertion failure means duplicate.

Access pattern: one insert per inbound event. Retention: pruned nightly once past the provider's own retry horizon.

Worth knowing: the check is a primary-key insert rather than select-then-insert, so two concurrent deliveries of the same event cannot both pass it.

History: added after a redelivered event during an incident applied a stale seat count twice.

Column processed_webhook_events.event_id (event_id text). The primary key, and therefore the guard itself. Duplicate delivery surfaces as an insert conflict rather than as a race between a select and an insert.

[context: Incident: Charged after cancelling] ## Incident: Charged after cancelling

[context: Operation: Secret rotation] ## Operation: Secret rotation
Runs quarterly for credentials, on demand for the rest. It replaces stored secrets and restarts consumers.

Safety property: database credentials rotate transparently. On failure: a bad rotation fails at boot rather than at first use.

Alerting: the signing secret is excluded from the routine schedule because rotating it signs every user out.

[context: Postmortem: Connections exhausted after scaling out] ## Postmortem: Connections exhausted after scaling out
Symptom: adding a fifth instance degraded all five. Cause: the effective connection ceiling is per-instance pool size times instance count, and the pool was not adjusted.

Fix: the per-instance pool was reduced. Lesson: scaling out sometimes requires scaling something else down, which is counter-intuitive enough to need writing down.

[context: Postmortem: Migration timed out mid-deploy] ## Postmortem: Migration timed out mid-deploy
Symptom: a backfill statement exceeded the timeout and left the roll halted. Cause: the backfill ran as a single statement across the whole table.

[context: Feature: Workspace creation] ## Feature: Workspace creation
Primary user: A team lead signing up for the first time. Creating a workspace provisions the tenancy, the first project and a trial subscription in a single transaction.

Rule: The slug is derived from the name and then fixed permanently.

Rule: The creator becomes the billing contact by default.

Rule: A trial starts immediately without a card.

Edge case: A creation that fails partway leaves nothing behind, because the whole provisioning runs in one transaction rather than as a sequence of steps.

Considered and rejected: An invite-first flow was tried and abandoned; teams wanted to see the product before deciding who else should be in it.

[context: Feature: Project list] ## Feature: Project list
Primary user: Anyone opening the product. Projects are listed newest first, with archived projects hidden behind a filter rather than removed.

Rule: Archived projects do not count toward the plan limit.

Rule: There is no manual ordering and no pinning.

Rule: The list is not paginated below a few hundred projects.

Edge case: A workspace over its limit after a downgrade still sees every project; only creation is blocked.

Considered and rejected: Manual ordering was requested repeatedly and declined, because it makes the list stateful per person and the sort order stops meaning anything shared.

The scrubbing script that prepares an analysis dump fails outright if a document body, email address or display name survives into its output.

[context: Feature: Document editing] ## Feature: Document editing
Primary user: A contributor writing up work. Documents are rich text saved on a debounce, with no explicit save action and no version history surfaced.

Rule: The byte size is recalculated on every save.

Rule: Concurrent edits are last-write-wins.

Rule: There is no draft state.

Edge case: Two people editing simultaneously will overwrite each other; this is a known limitation rather than a bug, and collaborative editing is the single largest piece of deferred work.

Considered and rejected: Operational transformation was scoped and deferred; the cost is considerable and the observed rate of genuine concurrent editing is low.

[context: Feature: Search] ## Feature: Search
Primary user: A contributor who knows something exists but not where. Full-text search across titles and bodies within the current workspace only.

Rule: Results never cross a workspace boundary.

Rule: Archived projects are excluded unless explicitly included.

Rule: Ranking is the database's own, with no custom weighting.

Edge case: Search quality degrades noticeably once a workspace passes a few thousand documents, which is the trigger for replacing it.

Considered and rejected: A dedicated search service was costed and deferred until the attachment feature makes it unavoidable.

[context: Feature: Dashboard] ## Feature: Dashboard
Primary user: Anyone, on arrival. A single screen summarising project count, document count, storage and plan state.

Rule: The whole screen is populated by one request.

Rule: The plan card is presentational and receives its data as a prop.

Rule: The limit notice appears only when the limit is actually reached.

Edge case: An earlier version had the plan card fetch independently, which produced a visible flash where the badge settled a beat after the rest of the page.

[context: Feature: Billing panel] ## Feature: Billing panel
Primary user: Whoever holds the company card. Shows plan, seats, paid-through date, storage used and recent invoices, with controls to change payment method or end the plan.

Rule: The cancellation control is present and quiet, never hidden.

Rule: The confirmation states exactly what access remains.

Rule: A payment problem is shown as recoverable, not as an ended plan.

Edge case: A workspace whose card has failed sees a payment-issue state; calling it expired would be inaccurate and produces cancellations that would not otherwise happen.

[context: Feature: Seat management] ## Feature: Seat management
Primary user: A team lead adding or removing people. Seat count changes take effect immediately and are prorated by the payment provider.

Rule: Seats cannot go below the number of active people.

Rule: Proration is never computed locally.

Rule: A seat change is a single quantity update upstream.

Edge case: Removing a person does not automatically reduce the seat count, because teams frequently re-add within days and the churn of proration events confuses the invoice.

Considered and rejected: Automatic seat reduction was tried and reverted after customers found their invoices unpredictable.

[context: Feature: Invitations] ## Feature: Invitations
Primary user: A team lead onboarding colleagues. An emailed link that expires, binding the recipient to one workspace.

Rule: An invitation is single-use.

Rule: Expiry is measured in days, not hours.

Rule: An invitation to an existing address in another workspace still works, because identity is per workspace.

Edge case: Someone already in the workspace who follows an invitation is silently sent to the workspace rather than shown an error.

Considered and rejected: Domain-based auto-join was declined; it surprises people and creates seats nobody chose to pay for.

[context: Feature: Notifications] ## Feature: Notifications
Primary user: Anyone with an email address on file. Three transactional emails only: an invitation, a payment failure, and a plan change.

Rule: Every message names the workspace.

Rule: There is no digest and no activity feed.

Rule: A payment failure goes to the billing contact alone.

# Observability handbook
How Meridian is instrumented, what is measured, and the conventions that keep the signal usable.
chunks.normText: # observability handbook how meridian is instrumented, what is measured, and the conventions that keep the signal usable.

chunks.text:
[context: What we measure and why] ## What we measure and why
Observability here is scoped to answering three questions quickly: is the service up, is it slow, and did a specific customer's action succeed. Everything in this handbook exists to serve one of those, and instrumentation that serves none of them is removed rather than left to accumulate.

The third question is the one that drives most of the design. Aggregate dashboards tell you a percentage failed; they rarely tell you which request, for which workspace, at which step. That is why request correlation is treated as infrastructure rather than as a debugging convenience.
chunks.normText: [context: what we measure and why] ## what we measure and why observability here is scoped to answering three questions quickly: is the service up, is it slow, and did a specific customer's action succeed. everything in this handbook exists to serve one of those, and instrumentation that serves none of them is removed rather than left to accumulate. the third question is the one that drives most of the design. aggregate dashboards tell you a percentage failed; they rarely tell you which request, for which workspace, at which step. that is why request correlation is treated as infrastructure rather than as a debugging convenience.

chunks.text:
[context: Structured logging] ## Structured logging
Every log line is JSON with a fixed envelope: timestamp, level, message, request id, workspace id where known, and a free-form context object. Free-form text logs are not accepted in review, because the search patterns that work against them stop working the moment someone rewords a message.

Prometheus scrapes the application every fifteen seconds, and no metric is permitted to carry a workspace identifier as a label.

Levels are used narrowly. Error means a human should look. Warn means something recovered but the recovery is worth knowing about. Info marks state transitions that a support engineer would want in a timeline. Debug is off in production and is not expected to be readable by anyone but its author.

Personally identifying data does not go into logs. Workspace and user identifiers are opaque UUIDs and are safe; email addresses, display names and document bodies are not, and the review checklist calls this out explicitly because it is the single most common finding.

chunks.text:
[context: Request correlation] ## Request correlation
The load balancer assigns an X-Request-Id when the client does not supply one. The application stores it in an AsyncLocalStorage context at the first middleware, and every logger call reads it from there rather than being passed it explicitly.

The identifier travels outward as well as inward. Stripe calls carry it as an idempotency key suffix, and SQL statements carry it in a leading comment so a slow query in pg_stat_statements can be traced back to the request that issued it.

The AsyncLocalStorage approach has one sharp edge worth knowing: a callback scheduled with setTimeout outside the request scope loses the context and logs without a request id. The retry sweep hit this and now establishes its own synthetic context per invoice.

chunks.text:
[context: Metrics] ## Metrics
Metrics are Prometheus-format and scraped every fifteen seconds. The cardinality budget is enforced in review: no metric may carry a workspace identifier as a label. That rule exists because an early seat-count gauge labelled by workspace grew to tens of thousands of series and made the whole scrape slow.

The four request metrics are count, duration histogram, in-flight gauge and error count, labelled by route template and status class. Route template, not path -- labelling by raw path is the other way to blow a cardinality budget.

Business metrics live alongside technical ones. Active subscriptions by status, invoice retry outcomes, and entitlement cache hit ratio are the three that have actually caught incidents.

The cardinality rule exists because an early seat-count gauge labelled by workspace grew to tens of thousands of series and slowed the entire scrape.

chunks.text:
[context: Tracing] ## Tracing
Tracing is sampled rather than exhaustive. The head-based sampler keeps a small percentage of ordinary requests and every request that ends in a 5xx, which gives useful coverage without the storage cost of full capture.

Spans are created at three levels: the HTTP request, each outbound call, and each database statement. Deeper instrumentation was tried and reverted; the extra spans made traces harder to read without answering a question the three levels could not.

The most valuable trace attribute has turned out to be the entitlement cache outcome. A slow request that missed the cache looks entirely different from a slow request that hit it, and without the attribute the two are indistinguishable in aggregate latency.

chunks.text:
[context: Alerting] ## Alerting
Alerts are written against symptoms, not causes. Nobody is paged because CPU is high; they are paged because the error rate crossed a threshold or the health check has been failing.

Every alert must name an action in its annotation. An alert whose runbook says investigate is not an alert, it is a dashboard, and it gets demoted to one.

The alert set is intentionally small. Five paging alerts cover availability, error rate, latency, webhook processing lag and database connection saturation. Anything else routes to a channel and waits for business hours.

chunks.text:
[context: Dashboards] ## Dashboards
There is one overview dashboard and one dashboard per subsystem. The overview is the only one anyone is expected to know by heart, and it fits on a single screen without scrolling, which is a constraint that has been defended more than once.

Panels are ordered by the question they answer rather than by data source. Availability first, then latency, then saturation, then the business counters. A newcomer reading top to bottom should be able to describe the system's state without being told what to look at.

chunks.text:
[context: Incident practice] ## Incident practice
The first action in an incident is to write in the channel what you are about to do, before doing it. This is slower for the individual and dramatically faster for the group, because it prevents two people from restarting the same thing.

Timelines are reconstructed from logs, not from memory. This is the payoff for the correlation work: a support ticket that names a workspace and a time yields the exact request path in a single query.

Reviews are blameless in the specific sense that the question is always what made the mistake easy rather than who made it. The grace-period access bug produced the entitlement test suite; the health-check outage produced the rule that liveness endpoints do not touch dependencies.

chunks.text:
# Platform engineering guide
Environments, build, migration, deployment, scheduled work and the operational rules that hold them together.
chunks.normText: # platform engineering guide environments, build, migration, deployment, scheduled work and the operational rules that hold them together.

chunks.text:
[context: Environments] ## Environments
There are three environments and they differ in exactly the ways you would expect and no others. Development runs locally against Docker Postgres and Redis. Staging runs the production image against a schema-identical database seeded from a scrubbed dump. Production runs four API instances behind a load balancer.

Staging shares the production Stripe account in test mode. This is worth calling out because it means staging webhooks and production webhooks are configured separately and carry different signing secrets, which has caught people out.

There is no shared development database. Every engineer runs their own, and the seed script is maintained as a first-class artefact rather than as something someone dumped once.

chunks.text:
[context: Build pipeline] ## Build pipeline
CI runs typecheck, lint and tests in parallel, then builds the container image only if all three pass. The parallel split matters because typecheck is the slowest of the three and running it after tests would add its duration to every failing run.

The image is built once and promoted. The artefact deployed to production is byte-identical to the one that passed staging, which removes an entire class of works-in-staging failure.

Build caching is layered so that a dependency change and a source change have very different costs. Lockfile-driven layers are cached aggressively; source layers are not cached at all, because a stale source layer is far more expensive than a slow build.

Staging shares the production Stripe account in test mode, so staging and production webhooks are configured as separate endpoints with different signing secrets.

chunks.text:
[context: Migrations] ## Migrations
Migrations run before the rolling restart, which means every migration must be backward compatible with the currently deployed code. Both versions run simultaneously during the roll, and a migration that breaks the old version breaks production for the duration.

The practical rule is that a schema change is split across releases. Adding a column is one release; writing to it is the next; reading from it and making it required is a third. Dropping a column is the same sequence in reverse.

There are no down-migrations outside development. The runner refuses to execute one when the environment is not development. Forward-fix is the only rollback path for schema, and rolling back the image is always safe because of the backward-compatibility rule above.

chunks.text:
[context: Deployment] ## Deployment
Deployment is a rolling restart, one instance at a time, waiting for the health check to pass before moving on. With four instances the roll takes a few minutes and the service stays available throughout.

The health check reports process liveness and configured environment. It deliberately does not touch Postgres or Redis. A dependency check here would mean a brief database blip pulls every instance out of the load balancer at once, converting a recoverable incident into a full outage.

Shutdown is graceful and ordered: stop accepting connections, finish in-flight requests, drain the connection pools, then exit. A hard deadline forces exit if draining stalls, because an instance that will not die blocks the roll.

chunks.text:
[context: Scheduled work] ## Scheduled work
Three cron jobs carry all the asynchronous work in the system. The invoice retry sweep runs every five minutes and pays invoices whose retry window has elapsed. The nightly maintenance job expires stale grace periods and prunes processed webhook events. The storage rollup warmer runs hourly.

Every job is idempotent and safe to run concurrently with itself. This is not aspirational: the scheduler occasionally double-fires, and jobs that assumed single execution were the source of two duplicate-charge incidents before the property was enforced.

Jobs log a start line, a finish line and a count. A job that finishes without logging a count is treated as a bug, because a silent job is indistinguishable from a job that did not run.

chunks.text:
[context: Secrets] ## Secrets
Secrets come from the platform secret store and are injected as environment variables at container start. Nothing reads a secret from disk, and no secret appears in an image layer.

Rotation cadence differs by secret because the blast radius differs. Database credentials rotate quarterly and transparently. The Stripe key rotates on demand. The session signing secret signs every user out when rotated, so it is changed during a maintenance window rather than on a schedule.

The environment schema is validated at boot and the process refuses to start on a bad configuration. Starting half-configured and failing on the first real request is strictly worse: it passes the health check and takes traffic.

[context: Capacity] ## Capacity
The connection pool ceiling is the binding constraint, not CPU. Each API instance holds a pool, so the effective connection count is the pool maximum multiplied by the instance count, and Postgres has a hard limit well below what four instances with a generous pool would request.

Scaling out therefore requires shrinking the per-instance pool, which is counter-intuitive enough that it is written down here. A fifth instance added without adjusting the pool exhausts connections and degrades all five.

Redis capacity has never been the constraint. The entitlement cache is small, short-lived and highly compressible.

chunks.text:
[context: Backups and recovery] ## Backups and recovery
Postgres takes a continuous archive with point-in-time recovery. The recovery objective is measured in minutes rather than hours, and the restore procedure is exercised quarterly against a scratch instance.

An untested backup is not a backup. The quarterly exercise has twice found a problem that would have mattered: once a missing extension in the restore environment, once a role that did not exist on the target.

The container image is built once and promoted unchanged, so the artefact running in production is byte-identical to the one that passed staging.

Redis is not backed up. Everything in it is derived and rebuilds on demand, which is a deliberate property of the cache design rather than an accepted risk.

chunks.text:
[context: Cost] ## Cost
The dominant line item is the database, followed by the API instances, followed by egress. Object storage and Redis are rounding errors at current scale.

The storage rollup cache was originally a performance fix and turned out to be a cost fix as well: the query it replaced was the single largest consumer of database CPU, and removing it from the request path measurably reduced the instance size required.

Cost review happens quarterly and looks for shape changes rather than percentages. A line item that grows with customer count is expected; one that grows with time is a leak.

chunks.text:
[context: On-call] ## On-call
The rotation is weekly and covers business hours plus paging outside them. The expectation is explicitly not that the on-call engineer fixes everything, but that they stabilise and escalate.

Handover is a written summary, not a conversation. Anything still open, anything that fired and self-resolved, and anything deployed late in the week goes in the note.

Alert volume is treated as a defect. A week with more than a handful of pages produces a review of the alerts themselves, not just of the incidents.

chunks.text:
# Meridian product specification
The complete product definition: who it is for, what it does, what it deliberately does not do, and why each boundary sits where it does.
chunks.normText: # meridian product specification the complete product definition: who it is for, what it does, what it deliberately does not do, and why each boundary sits where it does.

chunks.text:
[context: Product summary] ## Product summary
Meridian is a shared workspace for small engineering teams. It provides project boards, a document store scoped to each project, and per-seat billing. The product thesis is that teams of five to thirty do not need the configurability of a large project tool and are actively slowed by it.

The target customer is a team that has outgrown a shared document folder and has rejected a heavyweight tracker. They want structure without administration.
chunks.normText: [context: product summary] ## product summary meridian is a shared workspace for small engineering teams. it provides project boards, a document store scoped to each project, and per-seat billing. the product thesis is that teams of five to thirty do not need the configurability of a large project tool and are actively slowed by it. the target customer is a team that has outgrown a shared document folder and has rejected a heavyweight tracker. they want structure without administration.

chunks.text:
[context: Personas] ## Personas
The primary persona is a team lead who owns delivery but does not want to become a tool administrator. They set up the workspace, invite the team, and expect to spend no further time on configuration.

The secondary persona is an individual contributor who reads more than they write. Their experience is dominated by finding things, which is why search and the project summary get disproportionate design attention.

The third persona is whoever holds the company card. They appear rarely, care only about the billing screen, and judge the product by whether that screen is honest and legible.

chunks.text:
[context: Workspaces and projects] ## Workspaces and projects
A workspace is the tenancy boundary and the billing unit. Everything belongs to exactly one workspace and nothing crosses between them. There is no concept of a user who belongs to two workspaces with one identity; they sign in separately.

Projects live inside a workspace and hold documents. Projects can be archived, which hides them and removes them from limit counting without deleting anything. Archiving rather than deleting is the recommended path in the onboarding flow.

There is no project hierarchy. Nesting was specified, prototyped and cut, because the prototype showed teams spending time arranging the hierarchy instead of using it.

chunks.text:
[context: Documents] ## Documents
Documents are plain rich text scoped to a project. They are not files: there is no upload, no versioning UI and no binary storage. This is a deliberate narrowing and the most frequently requested change.

The document body is stored inline in the database with a byte-size column maintained alongside it, so storage can be summed without reading bodies.

Search is Postgres full-text over titles and bodies within a workspace. It is adequate at current document counts and is understood to be the first thing that will need replacing.

chunks.text:
[context: Plans and limits] ## Plans and limits
There are two plans. Free is capped and single-workspace. Team is per-seat, billed monthly in arrears, and removes the caps.

The caps are chosen to be genuinely usable rather than to force an upgrade. A small team can run indefinitely on free, and a meaningful number do. The upgrade trigger in practice is seat count and the desire for unlimited projects, not a wall.

Limits are enforced at creation time only. Exceeding a limit by a plan downgrade does not delete anything; it prevents creating more. Destroying customer data to enforce a billing state is not something the product does.

chunks.text:
[context: Billing experience] ## Billing experience
The billing screen shows plan, seats, paid-through date and storage used. The cancellation control is present, quiet, and below the details rather than hidden.

Project nesting was specified, prototyped and then cut, because the prototype showed teams spending their time arranging the hierarchy instead of using it.

Cancellation opens a confirmation that states plainly what access remains. Dark patterns in the cancellation flow are out of scope as a matter of policy, and the confirmation copy is reviewed alongside the code.

A workspace whose payment has failed sees a payment-issue state rather than an expired one. The distinction is real: the account is recoverable, and telling people their plan has ended when it has not produces cancellations that would not otherwise happen.

chunks.text:
[context: Onboarding] ## Onboarding
A new workspace starts on a trial rather than on free. The trial exists to let a team evaluate the uncapped experience, and it converts to free rather than expiring into nothing.

The onboarding checklist has four items and is dismissible. Longer checklists were tested and completed less often.

The single strongest activation signal is the second project. Teams that create one project are evaluating; teams that create two have adopted.

chunks.text:
[context: Mobile] ## Mobile
The mobile client is read-oriented. It shows the dashboard, project lists and document reading. Editing on mobile was specified and deferred.

Mobile cannot afford the round trips the web dashboard makes, so it reads a single denormalised summary endpoint versioned separately from the rest of the API. Versioning it separately means the payload can change for mobile without coordinating a web release.

Offline support is out of scope. The product is collaborative and a stale local view creates more confusion than it removes.

chunks.text:
[context: Notifications] ## Notifications
Notifications are email only and are deliberately sparse: an invite, a payment failure, and a plan change. There is no digest and no activity feed.

Every notification names the workspace, because people belong to more than one and an unattributed email is a support ticket.

Payment failure notification goes to the billing contact rather than to the whole workspace. Broadcasting a payment problem to a team is embarrassing for the person responsible and does not speed resolution.

chunks.text:
[context: Accessibility] ## Accessibility
The product targets WCAG 2.2 AA. The commitment is tested rather than asserted: keyboard traversal and screen-reader labelling are part of the review checklist for any interactive component.

The cancellation confirmation is a modal dialog with an explicit role and focus trap. Modals are the component most often shipped inaccessible, so this one is called out.

Colour is never the only carrier of meaning. Plan status is conveyed by label as well as by badge colour.

chunks.text:
[context: Analytics] ## Analytics
Product analytics answer activation and retention questions. They do not attempt to reconstruct individual behaviour, and no event carries document content.

The metric the team steers by is weekly active workspaces rather than weekly active users, because the product is bought and abandoned as a team.

Churn is analysed by cause rather than by rate. Cancellation and payment failure are entirely different failures with entirely different remedies, and collapsing them into one number hid that for two quarters.

chunks.text:
[context: Support] ## Support
Support has read access to workspace metadata and billing state, and can mint an impersonated session for a user within a workspace. They cannot read document bodies.

The most common ticket is a billing question, and the second most common is a sign-in problem caused by session invalidation after a password change. Both have runbook entries.

Support can extend a grace period directly. This is a supported action with a documented procedure rather than a database poke, because it happens often enough to deserve one.

[context: Roadmap and non-goals] ## Roadmap and non-goals
The nearest committed work is document file attachments, which is the most requested capability by a wide margin.

Single sign-on is specified and gated behind a flag. It is not on the near roadmap because the current customer size rarely demands it.

Explicit non-goals: time tracking, gantt charts, custom workflow states, and a public API. Each has been requested and each would move the product toward the category it was built to avoid.

[context: Feature: Document editing] ## Feature: Document editing
Primary user: A contributor writing up work. Documents are rich text saved on a debounce, with no explicit save action and no version history surfaced.

Rule: The byte size is recalculated on every save.

Rule: Concurrent edits are last-write-wins.

Rule: There is no draft state.

Edge case: Two people editing simultaneously will overwrite each other; this is a known limitation rather than a bug, and collaborative editing is the single largest piece of deferred work.

Considered and rejected: Operational transformation was scoped and deferred; the cost is considerable and the observed rate of genuine concurrent editing is low.

[context: Operation: Invoice retry sweep] ## Operation: Invoice retry sweep
Runs every five minutes. It pays invoices whose retry window has elapsed.

Safety property: idempotent and safe to run concurrently with itself. On failure: a failure increments the attempt counter and leaves the row in place.

Alerting: a sweep that logs no count is treated as a bug, because a silent job is indistinguishable from a job that did not run.

[context: Operation: Nightly maintenance] ## Operation: Nightly maintenance
Runs 03:15 UTC. It expires stale grace periods and prunes processed webhook events.

Safety property: both steps are bounded deletes with a limit. On failure: a partial run leaves work for the next night; nothing is lost.

Alerting: paged only if it fails on two consecutive nights.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Migration runner for Meridian.

Applies SQL files from migrations/ in filename order, tracking what has run in a
schema_migrations table. Intentionally minimal: no down-migrations outside
development, no dependency graph, no checksums beyond a warning.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import hashlib
import os
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import psycopg

MIGRATIONS_DIR = Path(__file__).parent.parent / "migrations"

def connect() -> psycopg.Connection:
    url = os.environ.get("DATABASE_URL")
    if not url:
        sys.exit("DATABASE_URL is not set")
    return psycopg.connect(url, autocommit=False)

def ensure_tracking_table(conn: psycopg.Connection) -> None:
    with conn.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute(
            """
            create table if not exists schema_migrations (
              filename    text primary key,
              checksum    text not null,
              applied_at  timestamptz not null default now()
            )
            """
        )
    conn.commit()

""" from __future__ import annotations import argparse import hashlib import os import sys from pathlib import path import psycopg migrations_dir = path(__file__).parent.parent / "migrations" def connect() -> psycopg.connection: url = os.environ.get("database_url") if not url: sys.exit("database_url is not set") return psycopg.connect(url, autocommit=false) def ensure_tracking_table(conn: psycopg.connection) -> none: with conn.cursor() as cur: cur.execute( """ create table if not exists schema_migrations ( filename text primary key, checksum text not null, applied_at timestamptz not null default now() ) """ ) conn.commit()

def applied(conn: psycopg.Connection) -> dict[str, str]:
    with conn.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute("select filename, checksum from schema_migrations")
        return dict(cur.fetchall())

def apply_pending(conn: psycopg.Connection, dry_run: bool) -> int:
    done = applied(conn)
    files = sorted(MIGRATIONS_DIR.glob("*.sql"))
    count = 0

for path in files:
        body = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        checksum = hashlib.sha256(body.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

if path.name in done:
            if done[path.name] != checksum:
                print(f"warning: {path.name} changed after being applied")
            continue

if dry_run:
            print(f"would apply {path.name}")
            count += 1
            continue

print(f"applying {path.name}")
        with conn.cursor() as cur:
            cur.execute(body)
            cur.execute(
                "insert into schema_migrations (filename, checksum) values (%s, %s)",
                (path.name, checksum),
            )
        conn.commit()
        count += 1

return count

def reset(conn: psycopg.Connection) -> None:
    """Drops and recreates the public schema. Refuses to run unless
    MERIDIAN_ALLOW_RESET is set to the literal string "yes-destroy-my-data"."""
    if os.environ.get("MERIDIAN_ALLOW_RESET") != "yes-destroy-my-data":
        sys.exit("refusing to reset: MERIDIAN_ALLOW_RESET is not set")
    with conn.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute("drop schema public cascade")
        cur.execute("create schema public")
    conn.commit()
    print("schema reset")

def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Meridian migration runner")
    parser.add_argument("--apply", action="store_true", help="apply pending migrations")
    parser.add_argument("--reset", action="store_true", help="drop and recreate schema")
    parser.add_argument("--dry-run", action="store_true", help="show pending only")
    args = parser.parse_args()

conn = connect() try: if args.reset: reset(conn) ensure_tracking_table(conn) if args.apply or args.dry_run: n = apply_pending(conn, dry_run=args.dry_run) print(f"{n} migration(s) {'pending' if args.dry_run else 'applied'}") finally: conn.close() if __name__ == "__main__": main()

import { router } from 'express'; import { z } from 'zod'; import { requiresession } from '../auth/middleware.js'; import { requireentitlement } from '../auth/permissions.js'; import { readsubscriptionstate, requestcancellation, shouldallowrenewal, } from '../billing/subscriptions.js'; import { listinvoices } from '../billing/invoices.js'; import { createcheckoutsession } from '../billing/stripe.js'; import { workspacestoragebytes } from '../database/queries.js'; export const billingrouter: router = router(); /** * current billing state for the settings screen and the dashboard card. * this is a read model only -- every rule about what a status means lives in * the billing and auth modules, not here. */ billingrouter.get('/state', requiresession, async (req, res) => { const workspaceid = req.session!.workspaceid; const [subscription, storage] = await promise.all([ readsubscriptionstate(workspaceid), workspacestoragebytes(workspaceid), ]);

res.json({ status: subscription.status, seats: subscription.seats, paidthrough: subscription.paidthrough, cancellationrequested: subscription.cancellationrequestedat !== null, storagebytes: storage, }); }); billingrouter.get('/invoices', requiresession, async (req, res) => { res.json({ invoices: await listinvoices(req.session!.workspaceid) }); }); billingrouter.post( '/checkout', requiresession, requireentitlement('billing:write'), async (req, res) => { const body = z.object({ seats: z.number().int().min(1).max(500) }).parse(req.body); res.json({ url: await createcheckoutsession(req.session!.workspaceid, body.seats) }); }, ); /** * cancellation entry point. records the customer's intent and lets the * subscription module decide what happens at the period boundary. */ billingrouter.post('/cancel', requiresession, async (req, res) => { await requestcancellation(req.session!.workspaceid); res.json({ ok: true }); });

/** * internal endpoint used by the renewal worker. the renewal worker calls this check before every charge attempt, and a false result is treated as a terminal outcome rather than something to retry. */ billingrouter.get('/renewal-allowed', requiresession, async (req, res) => { const state = await readsubscriptionstate(req.session!.workspaceid); res.json({ allowed: await shouldallowrenewal(state) }); });

import { router } from 'express'; import { z } from 'zod'; import { requiresession } from '../auth/middleware.js'; import { resolveentitlements } from '../auth/permissions.js'; import { countactiveprojects, querymany, queryone, execute } from '../database/queries.js'; import { readsubscriptionstate } from '../billing/subscriptions.js'; import { httperror } from '../app.js'; export const projectsrouter: router = router(); const free_tier_project_limit = 3; projectsrouter.get('/', requiresession, async (req, res) => { const rows = await querymany( `select id, name, archived_at, created_at from projects where workspace_id = $1 order by created_at desc`, [req.session!.workspaceid], ); res.json({ projects: rows }); }); projectsrouter.post('/', requiresession, async (req, res) => { const body = z.object({ name: z.string().min(1).max(200) }).parse(req.body); const granted = await resolveentitlements(req.session!.workspaceid);

if (!granted.has('projects:unlimited')) { const active = await countactiveprojects(req.session!.workspaceid); if (active >= free_tier_project_limit) { throw new httperror(402, 'project_limit_reached'); } } const row = await queryone<{ id: string }>( `insert into projects (workspace_id, name) values ($1, $2) returning id`, [req.session!.workspaceid, body.name], ); res.status(201).json({ id: row!.id }); }); /** * compact summary used by the dashboard cards and by the mobile client. * * the mobile app cannot afford the three round trips the web dashboard makes, * so this endpoint denormalises project counts, storage and billing status into * one response. the mobile dashboard reads this data from the endpoint /api/v2/project-summary, which is versioned separately from the rest of the api so the payload shape can change without breaking web clients. */ projectsrouter.get('/v2/project-summary', requiresession, async (req, res) => { const workspaceid = req.session!.workspaceid; const [active, subscription, granted] = await promise.all([ countactiveprojects(workspaceid), readsubscriptionstate(workspaceid), resolveentitlements(workspaceid), ]);

res.json({ activeprojects: active, projectlimit: granted.has('projects:unlimited') ? null : free_tier_project_limit, plan: { status: subscription.status, seats: subscription.seats, paidthrough: subscription.paidthrough, renewsautomatically: subscription.cancellationrequestedat === null && subscription.status === 'active', }, }); }); projectsrouter.post('/:id/archive', requiresession, async (req, res) => { const changed = await execute( `update projects set archived_at = now() where id = $1 and workspace_id = $2 and archived_at is null`, [req.params.id, req.session!.workspaceid], ); if (changed === 0) throw new httperror(404, 'project_not_found'); res.json({ ok: true }); });

import { router } from 'express'; import { z } from 'zod'; import { requiresession } from '../auth/middleware.js'; import { bumpsessionepoch, issuesession } from '../auth/auth.js'; import { queryone, execute } from '../database/queries.js'; import { httperror } from '../app.js'; export const usersrouter: router = router(); usersrouter.get('/me', requiresession, async (req, res) => { const user = await queryone( `select id, email, display_name, workspace_id from users where id = $1`, [req.session!.userid], ); if (!user) throw new httperror(404, 'user_not_found'); res.json(user); }); const updateschema = z.object({ displayname: z.string().min(1).max(120).optional(), password: z.string().min(12).optional(), }); usersrouter.patch('/me', requiresession, async (req, res) => { const body = updateschema.parse(req.body);

if (body.displayname) { await execute('update users set display_name = $2 where id = $1', [ req.session!.userid, body.displayname, ]); } if (body.password) { await execute('update users set password_hash = $2 where id = $1', [ req.session!.userid, await hashpassword(body.password), ]); // changing the password must not leave old tokens usable. await bumpsessionepoch(req.session!.userid); } res.json({ ok: true }); }); /** * password hashing. passwords are hashed with argon2id at 64 mib of memory and three iterations, tuned so a single hash costs roughly 90 milliseconds on the api instance type. */ async function hashpassword(plaintext: string): promise<string> { const { hash, argon2id } = await import('argon2'); return hash(plaintext, { type: argon2id, memorycost: 65_536, timecost: 3, parallelism: 1, }); }

usersrouter.post('/sign-out-everywhere', requiresession, async (req, res) => { await bumpsessionepoch(req.session!.userid); res.json({ ok: true }); }); usersrouter.post('/impersonate/:userid', requiresession, async (req, res) => { const target = await queryone<{ id: string; workspace_id: string }>( 'select id, workspace_id from users where id = $1', [req.params.userid], ); if (!target) throw new httperror(404, 'user_not_found'); if (target.workspace_id !== req.session!.workspaceid) { throw new httperror(403, 'cross_workspace_impersonation'); } res.json({ token: await issuesession(target.id, target.workspace_id) }); });
